title: A bare npm install resolved to a ten day old dev build
foundBy: a consuming agent, relayed by the repository owner: "latest: 0.2.1-dev.20260830023458.856ea8f — 30 Aug, stale pointer"

evidence.verified: `npm view @codesweep-ai/ui dist-tags` now reports `latest: 0.3.0` and `dev: 0.3.1-dev.20260909170256.1638d27`. Before the release it reported `latest: 0.2.1-dev.20260830023458.856ea8f`, a build from 2026-08-30. The 0.3.0 artefact carries shasum 064adf42f62515bada9b49b49f5cd96d27b2609f and an SLSA provenance attestation, so it came from the workflow rather than from a person.

details:
`npm install @codesweep-ai/ui`, which is the command README.md and INSTALL.md both give, resolved to `0.2.1-dev.20260830023458.856ea8f`. That build was ten days old and carried none of the work since.

`npm.yml` publishes with `--tag dev` and has done since its first commit, so nobody ever aimed `latest` at a development build. npm did. A package must carry a `latest`, so the registry populated it from the first publish regardless of the tag that publish named.

The workflow comment said `--tag dev` keeps `latest` where the last release left it. No release had ever been cut, so it stayed where the first publish put it. CONTRIBUTING said a dev build reaches only someone who asks for it, and every consumer who did not ask was getting one.

Every published version was a prerelease, so no semver range resolved either. A consumer writing `^0.2.0` matched nothing at all.

notes.text:
Cutting 0.3.0 was the fix, and it makes the CONTRIBUTING sentence true rather than requiring it to be rewritten.

The release changes nothing a consumer runs. The published 0.3.0 and the `0.3.1-dev.20260909170256.1638d27` build on the dev channel were compared file by file: 230 files each, and only `package.json` differs, in its `version` field. Both record the same commit in `dist/BUILD.json`. Anyone pinned to the dev build was already running 0.3.0's code.

`cs-ledger check` warns that the shasum quoted above is not a commit in this repository. That warning is correct to ignore and will not go away.

The string is npm's tarball checksum, not a git sha. The checker reads any long run of hex as a commit citation, which is LGR-013 in the ledger tool's own records. The shasum stays because it is what identifies the published artefact, and identifying it is the point of the evidence.
